title: Equivalence Relations (Äquivalenzrelationen) and Orders (Ordnungen)
summary: Equivalence relations (Äquivalenzrelationen) group objects into equivalence classes (Äquivalenzklassen); these classes form partitions (Partitionen) and can be viewed as a quotient (Quotient). Congruence modulo m (Kongruenz modulo m) is a standard example, and a representative system (Repräsentantensystem) selects one element from each class. Order relations (Ordnungsrelationen) arrange comparable objects; partial orders (partielle Ordnungen) need not make every pair comparable, while total orders (Totalordnungen) do. Strict orders (Striktordnungen), prefix, suffix, and infix orders (Präfix-, Suffix- und Infixordnungen), and lexicographic order (lexikographische Ordnung) are further examples. Finite orders can be represented clearly by Hasse diagrams (Hasse-Diagramme).
keyFacts: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
An equivalence class [a]ᵣ contains all elements related to a by relation R.
The quotient A/R is the set of all equivalence classes of R on A.
The equivalence classes of an equivalence relation form a partition of the underlying set.
Every partition defines an equivalence relation by relating elements exactly when they lie in the same block.
A representative system contains exactly one element from each equivalence class.
Congruence modulo m partitions ℤ into the m residue classes.
The coarsest partition has one block; the finest partition consists of singleton blocks.
A relation is an equivalence relation if and only if it is reflexive, transitive, and symmetric.
The reflexive-transitive closure of a reflexive and transitive relation is the relation itself.
The intersection of two equivalence relations is again an equivalence relation; its classes are the intersections of the corresponding classes.
The union of two equivalence relations is not transitive in general.
A total order is a partial order in which every pair of elements is comparable.
A strict order is asymmetric and transitive.
The converse of a partial order is also a partial order.
A Hasse-diagram relation has no loops or transitive edges; its reflexive-transitive closure is the given order.
For finite partially ordered sets, the Hasse diagram is obtained by first removing loops and then transitive edges.
Lexicographic order first compares common prefixes and otherwise decides at the first position where the words differ.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements: Which properties define an equivalence relation?
questions.explanation: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Antisymmetry is instead part of the definition of a partial order.

questions.prompt: Which of the following relations is a partial order on its underlying set but not an equivalence relation?
questions.explanation: ≤ is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. It is not symmetric, so it is not an equivalence relation; the other options are equivalence relations.

source.heading: 1. Zwei Arten von Relationen: „gleichwertig“ vs. „steht vor“

questions.prompt: Let $A=\{u,v,w,z\}$ be the set and $R$ the equivalence relation under which two elements are related exactly when they lie in the same block of the partition $\{\{u,w\},\{v,z\}\}$. $[u]_R$ denotes the set of all elements related to $u$. Complete: $[u]_R=\{\,___\,\}$.
questions.explanation: The class of $u$ contains exactly the elements in the same block as $u$. This block is $\{u,w\}$.

questions.prompt: What does the quotient A/R denote when R is an equivalence relation on A?

options.text: The set of all elements that are not related to any other element
The set of all equivalence classes [a]ᵣ for a ∈ A
One representative from each class, together with all loops
The set of all pairs in A × A that are not in R

questions.explanation: A/R consists of the equivalence classes of relation R. It is neither a set of pairs nor merely a representative system.

questions.prompt: A representative system for an equivalence relation contains exactly one element from each equivalence class.
questions.explanation: Selecting exactly one representative from each class is the defining property of a representative system.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about partitions and equivalence relations.

options.text: Every element of a partitioned set lies in exactly one block.
A partition may contain empty blocks.
The classes of an equivalence relation form a partition.
Every partition defines an equivalence relation by relating elements that lie in the same block.

questions.explanation: Equivalence classes form nonempty, disjoint blocks that together cover the underlying set. Empty blocks are not part of a partition.

questions.prompt: Which partition is the coarsest partition of a nonempty set A?

options.text: The partition with exactly two blocks
The partition {A} with exactly one block

questions.explanation: The coarsest partition groups all elements into one largest possible block. The finest partition, by contrast, consists of singleton blocks.

questions.prompt: Which properties define a partial order R?
questions.explanation: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. Asymmetry and transitivity define a strict order.

questions.prompt: Two elements a and b are called comparable with respect to R if ___ holds.

options.text: aRb and bRa only for a ≠ b

questions.explanation: Comparability requires at least one of the two directions. In a partial order, antisymmetry prevents both directions from holding at once for distinct elements.

questions.prompt: A total order is a partial order in which ___.

options.text: no two distinct elements are comparable

questions.explanation: A total order adds comparability of every pair of elements to the properties of a partial order.

questions.prompt: Which property, together with transitivity, characterizes a strict order?
questions.explanation: A strict order is asymmetric and transitive. Asymmetry rules out both loops and reverse edges.

questions.prompt: What remainder do you get when −7 is divided by 5? Choose the remainder from {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}.
questions.explanation: We have −7 = 5·(−2) + 3, so the remainder is 3. Therefore, −7 lies in the residue class 3 + 5ℤ.

questions.prompt: Which is a representative system for congruence modulo 4? Such a system contains exactly one representative of each residue.
questions.explanation: The residues of −2, −1, 0, and 1 modulo 4 are 2, 3, 0, and 1. Thus each of the four residues occurs exactly once.

questions.prompt: Each arrow represents an ordered pair in relation R. Which partition of {a,b,c} do the equivalence classes form?

context.content:
flowchart LR
  A["a"] --> A
  B["b"] --> B
  C["c"] --> C
  A --> B
  B --> A
context.caption: Arrow diagram of relation R

questions.explanation: a and b are related to each other in both directions and have loops; c has only its own loop. Therefore, the classes are {a,b} and {c}.

questions.prompt: Let R and S be equivalence relations on A. Select all statements that always hold.

options.text: If R ⊆ S, then [a]ᵣ ⊆ [a]ₛ for every a ∈ A.
R ∩ S is an equivalence relation.

questions.explanation: The intersection preserves reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity, and its classes are the intersections of the classes. The union, by contrast, is not transitive in general.

questions.prompt: On ℤ, let R be congruence modulo 2 and S be congruence modulo 5. Given 1R3 and 3S8, which statement holds for R ∪ S?

options.text: R ∪ S is transitive because 1R3 and 3S8.
R ∪ S is symmetric but not transitive because R and S are asymmetric.
R ∪ S is not transitive: 1 is related to 3 and 3 to 8, but 1 is not related to 8 by either relation.

questions.explanation: 1 and 3 have the same remainder modulo 2; 3 and 8 have the same remainder modulo 5. 1 and 8 are congruent neither modulo 2 nor modulo 5, so the union is not transitive.

questions.prompt: Let the divisibility relation on ℕ be defined by a|b exactly when a divides b. Which pair of numbers is incomparable?
questions.explanation: 8 does not divide 12, and 12 does not divide 8 either. In the other pairs, the smaller number divides the larger.

questions.prompt: Sort the words ε, b, aa, and ab lexicographically with a < b. Which order is ascending?
questions.explanation: The empty word is a prefix of every word, so it comes first. The first differing position decides the order between aa and ab, since a < b; both come before words beginning with b.

questions.prompt: The arrows show the immediate inclusion steps in P({u,v}). Which two sets are incomparable under ⊆?

context.content:
flowchart BT
  E["∅"] --> U["{u}"]
  E --> V["{v}"]
  U --> UV["{u,v}"]
  V --> UV
context.caption: Hasse diagram of the subset order on P({u,v})

questions.explanation: {u} does not contain v, and {v} does not contain u, so neither set is a subset of the other. The other pairs are comparable by inclusion.

questions.prompt: On $A=\{p,q,r\}$, let the partial order $R=\{(p,p),(q,q),(r,r),(p,q),(p,r),(q,r)\}$ be given. The corresponding strict relation is obtained by removing all loops $(x,x)$ from $R$. How many ordered pairs does this strict relation have?
questions.explanation: Removing the three loops leaves $(p,q)$, $(p,r)$, and $(q,r)$. Thus, the strict relation contains three ordered pairs.

questions.prompt: Consider the divisibility order on $D=\{1,2,3,6,12\}$: $xRy$ holds exactly when $x$ is a divisor of $y$. A Hasse edge goes from $x$ to $y$ when $x\mid y$, $x\ne y$ holds, and there is no $z\in D\setminus\{x,y\}$ such that $x\mid z$ and $z\mid y$. How many Hasse edges are there?
questions.explanation: The direct divisibility steps are $1\to2$, $1\to3$, $2\to6$, $3\to6$, and $6\to12$. The other divisibility pairs have at least one element between them.

questions.prompt: A 4-bit pattern 1111 represents the same residue modulo 16 in signed and unsigned representations. Which ordered value pair (unsigned, signed) corresponds to it?
questions.explanation: The bit pattern has unsigned value 15. In the signed range from −8 to 7, the corresponding representative is 15−16 = −1.

source.heading: Anwendung: signed vs. unsigned n-bit Integers

questions.prompt: If R is reflexive and transitive, then R = R*, where R* is the reflexive-transitive closure of R.
questions.explanation: R* adds pairs that are reachable reflexively and transitively from R. If R already has these properties, nothing needs to be added.

questions.prompt: Let S be any relation on A. Select all correct statements about (S ∪ Sᵀ)*.

options.text: It is always an equivalence relation.
It is obtained by considering S and all reverse edges, then taking reflexive-transitive reachability.
It is always a total order.
It is the smallest equivalence relation containing S.

questions.explanation: Adding the reverse edges makes the underlying connection symmetric; taking the reflexive-transitive closure makes it an equivalence relation. Every equivalence relation containing S must also contain this connection.

questions.prompt: Let S be any relation on A. Select all correct statements about S* ∩ (Sᵀ)*.

options.text: It is always an equivalence relation.
If S is symmetric, this intersection equals S*.
It is the smallest equivalence relation containing S.
It is the largest equivalence relation contained in S*.

questions.explanation: The intersection describes mutual reachability. It is always an equivalence relation, is the largest such relation contained in S*, and equals S* when S is symmetric.

questions.prompt: Let R and S be equivalence relations on A. Select all statements that always hold.

options.text: R ∪ S is always an equivalence relation.
R ∩ S is again an equivalence relation.
The class of a with respect to R ∩ S is [a]ᵣ ∩ [a]ₛ.
R ⊆ S holds exactly when [a]ᵣ ⊆ [a]ₛ for every a ∈ A.

questions.explanation: The properties of the intersection follow directly from those of R and S. The union may fail transitivity and is therefore not always an equivalence relation.

questions.prompt: For an equivalence relation R, suppose c ∈ [a]ᵣ ∩ [b]ᵣ. What follows?

options.text: R is not an equivalence relation.

questions.explanation: Two equivalence classes that share an element are the same class. Equivalence classes are therefore either equal or disjoint.

questions.prompt: Let R be a partial order. Select all statements about the dual order Rᵀ that always hold.

options.text: R and Rᵀ have the same incomparable pairs.
Rᵀ is also a partial order.
If R is a total order, then Rᵀ is also a total order.

questions.explanation: Reversing all arrows preserves reflexivity, antisymmetry, and transitivity. It reverses the direction of comparable pairs but leaves incomparable pairs incomparable.

questions.prompt: For a path π = v₀v₁…vₖ, a prefix is an initial segment that has the same ___ as π.

options.text: Set of edges in reverse order

questions.explanation: A prefix starts at the same start as the path and may end earlier. A suffix, by contrast, is a final segment with the same destination.

source.heading: Präfix, Suffix und Infix bei Pfaden und Relationen

questions.prompt: Why does (ℚ, ≤) have no Hasse diagram in the sense of a relation consisting of immediate successor edges?

options.text: Because for p < q, the rational number (p+q)/2 always lies between them
Because loops are required in a Hasse relation
Because ≤ on ℚ is not reflexive
Because ℚ is not a partially ordered set

questions.explanation: Between any two distinct rational numbers there is another rational number. Therefore, there are no immediate successor edges that are not transitive.

questions.prompt: What conditions must a relation S satisfy to be a Hasse diagram of the partial order R? Select all correct statements.

options.text: S contains all pairs in R.

questions.explanation: A Hasse diagram omits loops and edges that can be inferred transitively, but reflexive-transitive reachability must reconstruct the entire order.

questions.prompt: The edges show immediate inclusion steps among equivalence relations on {1,2,3}. Which statement follows from the diagram?

context.caption: Inclusion order of the equivalence relations on {1,2,3}

options.text: The finest partition is at the top and the coarsest at the bottom.
The order is total because every relation is a partition.
There is only one middle partition.
The three middle partitions are pairwise incomparable.

questions.explanation: Each middle partition lies between the finest and coarsest partitions, but none of the middle partitions refines another. Thus, the inclusion order is partial but not total.

questions.prompt: Which statement about two algebraic expressions can be true even though they are different strings?

options.text: An equivalence relation cannot compare expressions.
Different strings must always have different values.
Expressions are equivalent only if they are identical character by character.
They can have the same value for every input.

questions.explanation: For example, (x+y)² and x²+2xy+y² are different expressions that have the same value for all real x,y. The relation considers meaning rather than notation.

source.heading: Weitere wichtige Äquivalenzrelationen: Terme, Formeln, Programme

questions.prompt: Let A = {1,2,3,4} and P = {{1,4},{2},{3}}. Define xRy exactly when x and y lie in the same block of P. Select all correct statements.
questions.explanation: Elements are related exactly when they share a block. Thus, the class of 4 is {1,4}, and the quotient consists of the three blocks.

source.heading: Fakten: Äquivalenzrelationen und Partitionen gehören zusammen

questions.prompt: The 5-bit pattern 11101 has unsigned value 29 and represents the same class modulo 32 in signed and unsigned representations. Which value pair (unsigned, signed) is correct?
questions.explanation: The unsigned value is 29. In the 5-bit signed range from −16 to 15, the corresponding representative is 29−32 = −3.

source.heading: Anwendung: signed vs. unsigned n-bit Integers

questions.prompt: The arrows are immediate divisibility steps among the divisors of 12. Which numbers are incomparable in the divisibility order?

context.caption: Hasse diagram of the divisors of 12 under divisibility

questions.explanation: 4 does not divide 6, and 6 does not divide 4. The other listed pairs are comparable because the smaller number divides the larger.

source.heading: Teilbarkeit auf [10] und auf den Teilern von 30

questions.prompt: Two words are conjugate if one is obtained from the other by a cyclic shift. Which set is the conjugacy class of `abca`?
questions.explanation: Cutting at each possible position and then swapping the two parts gives abca, bcaa, caab, and aabc. These rotations form the class.

questions.prompt: A path consists of the vertices v₀v₁v₂v₃v₄. What is the relationship of the segment v₁v₂v₃ to the whole path?

options.text: It is a prefix but not an infix.
It is neither a prefix, suffix, nor infix.
It is a suffix but not an infix.
It is an infix, but neither a prefix nor a suffix.

questions.explanation: v₁v₂v₃ is a contiguous segment and therefore an infix. It does not start at v₀ or end at v₄, so it is neither a prefix nor a suffix.

questions.prompt: The arrows form a relation S on {1,2,3,4}. S* allows paths of length zero or more. The equivalence relation S* ∩ (Sᵀ)* groups exactly the vertices that can reach each other. Which quotient results?
questions.explanation: 1 and 2 can reach each other, as can 3 and 4. There is a path from the first group to the second, but not back, so there are two classes.

questions.prompt: Sort ε, ba, aa, ab, and b lexicographically with a < b. Which order is ascending?
questions.explanation: The empty word is a prefix of every word. Next come the words beginning with a, followed by those beginning with b; among the latter, b comes before its longer prefix extension ba.

questions.prompt: Define a relation on expressions by t₁Rt₂ exactly when both expressions have the same value for all real inputs. What holds for (x+y)² and x²+2xy+y²?

options.text: They are related only when x = y.
They are not related because their notations differ.
They are different strings, but they are related by R.
They cannot be compared by an equivalence relation.

questions.explanation: The two expressions are written differently, but they are equivalent by expansion and have the same value for all real x,y. Here, the relation groups different notations with the same meaning.

source.heading: Weitere wichtige Äquivalenzrelationen: Terme, Formeln, Programme

questions.prompt: Let A = {1,2,3}, P₁ = {{1,2},{3}}, and P₂ = {{1,2,3}}. R₁ and R₂ relate exactly those elements that lie in the same block of P₁ and P₂, respectively. Which inclusion statement holds?
questions.explanation: Every pair in a common P₁ block is also in the same P₂ block. P₂ additionally groups 1, 2, and 3 together, so R₁ is a proper subrelation of R₂.

questions.prompt: People are ordered by score: xRy exactly when x has fewer points than y. Then incomparability is an equivalence relation that groups people with the same score.
questions.explanation: Two people are incomparable under the strict score order exactly when they have the same number of points. Equality of scores is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

questions.prompt: How many edges does the Hasse diagram of the inclusion order on P({1,2,3}) have?
questions.explanation: Each Hasse edge adds exactly one missing element to a subset. For each of the three elements, there are four subsets to which it can be added, giving 3·4 = 12 edges.

levels.title: In practice: Relationships in everyday life

questions.prompt: A shift planner records hours across multiple days. For time of day, 07:00 and 31:00 are treated as equal. Which relation describes this grouping?

options.text: Total order by time of day

questions.explanation: The hour values differ by 24 and therefore have the same remainder modulo 24. This creates equivalence classes of equal times of day.

questions.prompt: A photo app groups images together exactly when they have the same width and height. What do these groups form mathematically?

options.text: A Hasse diagram of the resolutions
A lexicographic order of the image names
A total order of the photos by file size
Equivalence classes that divide the photos into a partition

questions.explanation: Having the same width and height is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. The groups are equivalence classes that divide all photos into disjoint blocks.

source.heading: Fakten: Äquivalenzrelationen und Partitionen gehören zusammen

questions.prompt: A sensor stores its counter reading as a residue modulo $2^8$. How many different readings can it display?
questions.explanation: Eight bits have $2^8$ possible patterns. Thus, there are 256 residue classes and correspondingly many different displayed counter readings.

source.heading: Anwendung: signed vs. unsigned n-bit Integers

questions.prompt: An algebra tool groups expressions over the integers if they have the same value for every integer $x$. Then $x+0$ and $x$ belong to the same equivalence class. Is this true?
questions.explanation: For every integer $x$, $x+0=x$ holds. Equivalent expressions can therefore be grouped into equivalence classes.

source.heading: Weitere wichtige Äquivalenzrelationen: Terme, Formeln, Programme

questions.prompt: In a release plan, a task is either the same as another task or must be completed before it. The dependencies are consistent and transitive; independent tasks may be incomparable. Which type of order describes this relation?
questions.explanation: The relation is reflexive (every task is related to itself), antisymmetric (two distinct tasks cannot each come before the other), and transitive. Since independent tasks may be incomparable, it is partial but not total.

questions.prompt: A running counter displays only its last four digits, from `0000` to `9999`. How many different displays, or residue classes modulo 10,000, are there?
questions.explanation: Each of the four positions has ten possibilities. This gives $10^4=10.000$ displays; identical last four digits correspond to the same residue class modulo 10,000.

questions.prompt: In a game tech tree, some unlocks depend indirectly on one another. To keep the diagram clear, only direct unlock steps are shown; connections that can be inferred indirectly are omitted. What is this representation of a partial order called?
questions.explanation: A Hasse diagram shows the immediate relations of a partial order. Transitive edges and loops are omitted, but can still be inferred from paths.

questions.prompt: Three distinguishable photos are to be divided into arbitrary unlabeled groups. The order of the groups does not matter. How many different partitions are possible?
questions.explanation: There is one partition into three singleton groups, three partitions with exactly one pair, and one group containing all three photos. In total, there are five partitions.

source.heading: Fakten: Äquivalenzrelationen und Partitionen gehören zusammen

questions.prompt: A contacts app sorts strings over the alphabet $a<b<c$. At the first position where two strings differ, the alphabet order decides. If one string is a prefix of the other, the shorter comes first. Which concept does this describe?
questions.explanation: Lexicographic sorting decides at the first differing position. If one string is a prefix of the other, the shorter comes first.

questions.prompt: A web server checks strings as URL paths. A path is a prefix of another if its characters occur at the beginning of the other path; for example, `/shop` is a prefix of `/shop/item/8`. Which relation describes this?
questions.explanation: A prefix occurs at the beginning of a string. The prefix relation is a partial order: two paths need not be prefixes of each other.

source.heading: Präfix, Suffix und Infix bei Pfaden und Relationen
